name: Black Brant IX
summary: A two-stage NASA sounding rocket: a Terrier booster under a Black Brant V motor. It flies straight up to about 300 km for a few minutes of science above the atmosphere, then the payload falls back under a parachute. Black Brant IXs have flown since 1982. Times and figures are typical; each mission differs.

info.summary: The booster: a surplus US Navy Terrier missile motor that gets the rocket off the rail fast.
info.purpose: Burns for about six seconds, kicking the rocket up to speed so the Black Brant stage can start well above the ground. Then it simply falls away.
info.funFact: Terrier motors were built in the 1950s and 60s to launch ship-borne anti-aircraft missiles. Sounding rockets gave thousands of surplus ones a second life.

info.summary: A solid-fuel rocket motor: a steel case packed with a rubbery propellant.
info.purpose: Solid motors can't be throttled or switched off once lit, but they are simple, reliable and can sit in storage for years.

info.summary: Four large fins at the tail of the booster.
info.purpose: Keep the rocket stable and spin it slowly as it climbs, which evens out small misalignments in thrust. Sounding rockets have no guidance system steering them.
info.funFact: The fins are canted by a fraction of a degree. That tiny angle is enough to spin the whole rocket several times a second.

info.summary: A short ring joining the two stages.
info.purpose: Holds the stages together during the boost, then lets go so drag can pull the spent Terrier away.

info.summary: The sustainer stage: a Black Brant V motor, the workhorse of the Canadian-designed Black Brant family.
info.purpose: After a short coast, it lights and burns for about half a minute, carrying the payload out of the atmosphere at several times the speed of sound.
info.funFact: The Black Brant family grew out of solid-propellant research in Canada starting in 1958.

info.summary: A long, thin solid motor, about 5.6 m from end to end.
info.purpose: Does the real work of the flight: by burnout, about 46 seconds after launch, the rocket is fast enough to coast to around 300 km.

info.summary: Smaller fins on the second stage.
info.purpose: Keep the upper stage pointing nose-first and spinning while it burns.

info.summary: The science section: instruments, their electronics, and the system that brings them home.
info.purpose: Everything the flight is for. Payloads typically weigh a few hundred kilograms and are recovered, refurbished and often flown again.

info.summary: Telescopes, particle detectors or other experiments, depending on the mission.
info.purpose: Make a few minutes of observations from above the atmosphere: ultraviolet and X-ray light from the Sun and stars, or the particles inside the aurora, none of which reach the ground.
info.funFact: Students and early-career scientists often build these payloads. A sounding rocket is one of the cheapest ways to get an instrument into space.

info.summary: The section that holds the packed parachute and its deployment hardware.
info.purpose: Senses when the payload has fallen back into thick air and pushes the parachute out.

info.summary: A large parachute, packed tight until the very end of the flight.
info.purpose: Slows the payload to a gentle landing so the instruments can be recovered and flown again.
info.funFact: After landing, the payload is usually picked up by helicopter or truck. From White Sands, it's often back in the lab the same day.

info.summary: The pointed cover that protects the instruments on the way up.
info.purpose: Cuts through the air during the boost, then is ejected once the rocket is above the atmosphere so the instruments can see out.

events.title: Countdown
events.caption: Final checks at the launch range. Sounding rockets launch from a rail, angled slightly to allow for the wind so the payload lands inside the range.

events.title: Terrier ignition
events.caption: The Terrier booster fires for about six seconds, accelerating the rocket off the rail at well over 10 g.

events.title: Terrier separation
events.caption: The spent Terrier drops away, pulled back by air drag. The upper stage coasts for a few seconds before lighting its own motor.

events.title: Black Brant ignition
events.caption: The Black Brant V motor ignites and burns for about half a minute, pushing the payload out of the atmosphere.

events.title: Burnout
events.caption: The motor is spent. From here the rocket simply coasts upward like a thrown ball, slowing all the way to the top.

events.title: Despin
events.caption: Weights on cables unreel from the payload to slow its spin (a "yo-yo despin"), so the instruments can point steadily.

events.title: Nose cone ejected
events.caption: The nose cone pops off, uncovering the instruments now that there is almost no air left to protect them from.

events.title: Payload separation
events.caption: The empty motor separates. The payload flies on alone, and above about 100 km the science window begins: several minutes of near-weightlessness and a clear view of space.

events.title: Apogee
events.caption: The highest point, typically around 300 km, almost as high as the International Space Station. But the payload is only going up, not sideways, so it falls straight back.

events.title: Re-entry
events.caption: The payload falls back into the atmosphere. Air resistance builds quickly and slows it from several kilometres per second.

events.title: Parachute deploys
events.caption: With the payload slowed by the air, the parachute opens for a gentle descent.

events.title: Touchdown
events.caption: About fifteen minutes after launch, the payload lands. The experiment's data was already radioed to the ground during the flight; now the hardware comes home too.

sources.title: Designation Systems: Bristol of Canada Black Brant
